messages.author: 88c2f7593fc46db6
messages.subject: suspicious model fit
parts:
#Sensation Seeking
CLPM1_SS <- '
            #Gerichtete Pfade
    totaluseqt_T2 ~ AR11 * totaluseqt + CL21 * SRPwoc3qt + CL31 * UPPS_SS_qt
    SRPwoc3qt_T2 ~ AR22 * SRPwoc3qt + CL12 * totaluseqt + CL32 * UPPS_SS_qt
    UPPS_SS_qt_T2 ~ AR33 * UPPS_SS_qt + CL13 * totaluseqt + CL23 * SRPwoc3qt
   
    # Kovarianzen zwischen den Variablen zu T2
  totaluseqt ~~ SRPwoc3qt
  totaluseqt ~~ UPPS_SS_qt
  SRPwoc3qt ~~ UPPS_SS_qt
  totaluseqt_T2 ~~ SRPwoc3qt_T2
  totaluseqt_T2 ~~ UPPS_SS_qt_T2
  SRPwoc3qt_T2 ~~ UPPS_SS_qt_T2
'
fit_SS <- sem(data = Gesamtdatensatz, model = CLPM1_SS, estimator="MLM", se="robust")
summary(fit_SS, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)

I computed a cross-lagged panel model in lavaan with the code above. The resulting model has CFI=1 and RMSEA=0 which is not a desirable result, I guess, since it either hints on overfitting or a general problem with my model, right? Did I make a mistake? The path coefficients seem to make sense and I based the model on the underlying theory, so I am not sure what to change?

messages.author: b8fd92e5e3662745
messages.subject: Re: suspicious model fit
parts:
You've created an exactly identified regression problem. Each triplet of the variables at time 1 and time 2 is fully correlated by the virtue of the second set of statements, and all nine cross-covariances are modeled as regression coefficients. You don't need lavaan for this, you would get pretty much the same answer with multivariate regression (multivariate == several outcome variables with the same regressors). The first google search link shows how this works: https://library.virginia.edu/data/articles/getting-started-with-multivariate-multiple-regression. Econometricians had honed that kind of stuff in 1950s (see simultaneous equation models in some older econometrics textbooks; the black Wooldridge "Cross-sectional and Panel Data" is a good universal reference) although they don't have time to teach that stuff anymore, in favor of the causal inference. As such, it would be immaterially different from running OLS / lm() on each equation (there are efficiency gains / smaller standard errors to the extent that the residuals at time 2 are really correlated; if they aren't, the results are equivalent).

This is not to say that this is a good model or a bad model -- as you correctly surmised, you don't have any ability to test the fit, so we cannot really tell. You can drop T2 correlations, but it would only tell you how good the model is in terms of the T2 correlations. If you seriously want to consider different ways to assess your fit, you would want to go back to regression formulation and look at the standard stuff like residual / influence diagnostics.
